newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS - Canadian markets brace for U.S. rate hike.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Canadian markets brace for U.S. rate hike.

text.p: Canadian financial markets sank this week to their lowest levels in months on investor concerns that U.S. interest rates would rise next Tuesday while the Bank of Canada kept Canadian rates steady.

The Canadian dollar reached its lowest level against the U.S. dollar in more than a year. Canadian T-bills traded with the highest yields since October and stocks and long bonds fell to their weakest levels since January.

"What we're doing now is building in the fact that most people expect that the Bank (of Canada) isn't going to follow (a U.S. rate hike)," said Michael Manford, chief economist with Scotia Capital Markets. "Right now nobody wants to step in."

Testimony by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Thursday helped solidify a growing belief among investors that the Fed's rate-setting Open Market Committee would tighten by 25 basis points when it met on Tuesday.
Although a U.S. rate hike in itself would be largely a negative for financial markets, such a move would have special implications for Canada, analysts said.
Last year, the Bank of Canada began charting a so-called "made-in-Canada" interest rate policy, dropping short-term interest rates 11 times compared with one rate cut by the Fed.
Canada's key bank rate, a benchmark of short-term Canadian rates, is now at 3.25 percent, compared with a U.S. Federal funds rate of 5.25 percent.
Analysts said investors were concerned that a U.S. rate hike would widen the difference in short-term interest rates and pressure the Canadian dollar and T-bills.
Higher administered interest rates tend to strengthen a country's currency by luring capital into instruments denominated in that currency.

Expectations that the Bank of Canada would not match a Fed hike were fueled on Tuesday when Governor Gordon Thiessen told a Senate committee that Canada's improved finances had given the central bank room to maneuver in response to possible U.S. rate rises.

"Gordon Thiessen has pretty well come out and said we're not going to follow them on the first round," said Josh Mendelsohn, chief economist with Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. "Investors are basically saying if he's not going to follow them and the Canadian dollar really doesn't have that much (reason) to go up at this point, why in God's name are we going to go into Canadian assets?"

Analysts said the major risk now was that the Canadian dollar could sell off sharply in response to a U.S. rate hike. That would force the Bank of Canada to hike Canadian rates one or possibly several times in order to defend the currency.
Analysts said the positive fundamentals of the Canadian dollar were intact and that there was so much bad news priced into the unit, it could rally sharply if the Fed did not hike.
"If the Fed didn't move next week you would find the Canadian dollar coming back and probably coming back a fair bit," said CIBC's Mendelsohn.
